title: Best Vibe Coding tool in 2026?
author: Devizzlmao
selftext:
So I've been using Rosebud for a year now and it did get much better over time. Been able to develop quite a complex game prototype with numerous, interconnected systems.

I am wondering what tools you guys use and what tool you consider the best to date?

comments.author: d-czar
comments.body:
Have you tried the Unity mcp? It’s free and open source and has evolved a ton in the last year. Makes building in Unity so much easier


https://github.com/CoplayDev/unity-mcp

replies.author: SaltAddictedMan
replies.body: Curious, how is this different than Bezi and claude code? Does it just made claude code better? Sounds super interesting.

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body:
For one thing it’s free and open source — Bezi costs $20/mo for lowest tier. 

As far as what it does: yes, it’s like giving Claude Code a powerful Swiss Army knife designed specifically for Unity, that lets Claude do a bunch of stuff in Unity really fast. Otherwise Claude has to tinker around and write its own tools to do things in Unity, which is more expensive and makes it reinvent the wheel every time. So if you tell Claude “build a tree in Unity with a brown trunk and green leaves and make it drop 5 red apples every minute”, Claude can just trigger the pre-built mcp tools to those things, rather than writing a bunch of code from scratch to tell Unity how to do it.

replies.author: SaltAddictedMan
replies.body: Amazing, I am so glad I found your post before I paid for Bezi

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body: Let me know if it works for you, will be curious what you think!

replies.author: HONGSHIreddit
replies.body: I haven't used Coplay personally but I have a great experience with Bezi. Bezi also looks at context of your project files so it doesn't just create code out of it's booty. The payment aspect is definitely something people tend to look at but I personally think it's a worthy investment if you're serious about game development. Not only does it create code for you, you can also ask it to break down the script so you can actually learn while you make your games.

replies.author: Okoear
replies.body:
Have you tried to do anything remotely complicated with Unity MCP such as interacting with complex UIs ect ? 

Hasn't been too successful for me.

replies.author: doorknob123
replies.body:
Bezi has a free trial so you can compare it to other tools. I tried the Unity MCP and it was cool if you want to really quickly build simple prototypes, but anything more complicated and it just kinda falls apart. If you’re optimizing for speed over everything then yea it’s fine for that.

I’m building a small game with a publisher rn and im using Bezi to help with some of the areas that I don’t have the most experience in like architecture and networking, so Bezi isn’t really a “vibe coding” tool in that regard, but it’s great for getting things to a external production standard. That being said I still also use Claude Code when I need to get deep into scripting.

I feel like the limitation with things like Rosebud and more traditional vibe coding tools is that their usefulness deteriorates after the prototype phase

comments.author: Roguelikeenjoyer88
comments.body: Bezi is my choice, been using it 6 months now. Others have mentioned the cost but really 20$ is such a small monthly price for how much it does. The thing I really like about it is that I don't feel alone anymore when I work, it's a perfect assistant. It's not as much a vibe coder.

comments.author: HONGSHIreddit
comments.body:
Personally, I've been really enjoying using Bezi for my projects.

I'm not a coder by any means of the definition, but it has allowed me to work on my personal projects and I have no complaints. The best thing I feel that is super beneficial to me as a vibe coder is that I'm not just creating things, I'm also slowly learning about debugging, thinking like an engineer (hopefully), and actually learning about things they don't go into great details with in tutorials.

The fact you can get scripts made and ask why it works is like getting the product and getting the behind the scenes knowledge. I'm not really great at retaining all the info it gives me but I'm picking up things little by little.

comments.author: Izkimar
comments.body:
spawn.co is the best platform for vibe coding games imo if you don't care about shipping projects to steam or your own site, since they handle all of the distribution.

Their games are multiplayer supported by default. Their content engine generates all of the assets. Though you can utilize your own as well. 

They just finished an engine overhaul recently and the new version is coming together very quickly. 

The team is also super responsive to feedback and always working to improve things quickly. I've been making games on their platform for awhile now and I think it's definitely worth checking out.

comments.author: genzbossishere
comments.body: most of them have gotten good enough that the difference shows up once projects get bigger, not at the start. whats worked better for me is separating planning from generation. if the idea, scope, and sequence are clear, a lot of tools feel interchangeable. i use braingrid in that phase just to keep intent and tasks straight before any code gets written. tools keep changing year to year. having a clear plan tends to last longer

comments.author: hoolieeeeana
comments.body: Most vibe coding tools feel fine until deployment, and having hosting handled in one place like Hostinger made my workflow smoother.. where does your build process usually slow down?

comments.author: bonnieplunkettt
comments.body: Sounds like Rosebud has given you a lot of flexibility for systems and logic, which is great to hear. Have you ever used Wix’s editor and Velo for prototype interfaces or backend logic and compared how quickly you can iterate?

comments.author: Techprohelper
comments.body: I’ve tried a few vibe coding tools alongside Copilot and Cursor, and YouWare feels best for idea-first building you describe what you want, it generates working app/web code with live preview and quick deploy. It’s not ideal for very complex custom logic, but for fast prototyping and turning concepts into something usable quickly, it’s genuinely smooth and enjoyable to use.

comments.body: [removed]

comments.author: b0red
comments.body: For game-adjacent stuff: Cursor or Windsurf for actual code. For functional tools (dashboards, portals, management systems): Taskade Genesis lets you describe what you want and builds it with AI agents included. Different category than code-gen but works well for the "describe and build" workflow.

comments.author: genzbossishere
comments.body: rosebud is solid, especially if youre deep into game prototypes and for more general app building, i see most people bouncing between claude + cursor or claude + a ui builder depending on what theyre shipping personally i think “best” depends on whether you separate planning from generating. we knew that tools change every few months, but having a clear spec first makes any of them perform better. sometimes thats just a clean doc, sometimes something like braingrid to structure flows before handing it to claude and once that part is settled, the model choice matters a lot less.

comments.author: genzbossishere
comments.body: i dont think theres a single best tool anymore. claude + cursor is still solid for bigger projects, gemini’s been getting better for quick iteration too the bigger difference in 2026 feels like workflow, not model. having a clear spec before generating code matters more than switching tools. ill outline features in a doc or braingrid first, then let claude or cursor implement. once the plan is tight, most top tools feel pretty close

comments.author: Klutzy-Challenge-610
comments.body: most tool are competent rn, difference usually comes from workflow, not model and one solid coding tool, clear repo structure, small scoped tasks. define systems and interactions first, sometimes in a short doc or something structured like braingrid, then implement piece by piece. for complex game systems especially, planning dependencies before generating saves a lot of refactor pain later. consistency matters more than chasing every new release.

comments.author: whatever_happened
comments.body: I still use a mix rather than relying on one tool, usually Claude Code or Cursor for deeper logic and iteration, then something like Replit or Bolt when I want to spin something up quickly. That setup holds up better once projects get more complex. I’ve also had a few colleagues mention an early access tool called PullSight that focuses more on planning, testing, and reviewing code before deployment instead of just generating it. Looks like it has good potential and I already applied for early access.
